summary:
Sphere X is a public-facing web platform that transforms time-series observations from NASA’s SPHEREx mission into an accessible, interactive experience for exploring how the sky changes over time.

Users can enter Right Ascension and Declination coordinates, retrieve available SPHEREx observations for that region, and explore them as a temporal sequence. Tools such as playback, Blink, Overlay, and Difference make it easier to identify apparent motion, brightness variations, or other visible changes between observations.

Sphere X goes beyond visualization by combining automated assistance with human exploration. The system can highlight sources that show possible motion or temporal change, while users can also manually select something they find interesting and create a structured report for further review. It does not claim to automatically identify astronomical anomalies; instead, it helps people recognize and investigate meaningful changes in the data.

An AI-powered guide provides contextual explanations, interactive tutorials, and step-by-step assistance based on what the user is currently viewing.

By combining SPHEREx data, scientific visualization, AI guidance, and human-in-the-loop participation, Sphere X makes astronomical exploration more understandable, engaging, and accessible to scientists, students, and curious citizens alike.
details:
Sphere X turns SPHEREx time-series data into an interactive environment for exploring how the sky changes. Instead of requiring users to download and process astronomical files manually, the platform allows anyone to enter Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec), retrieve available observations for that region from NASA/IPAC IRSA, and explore them visually across time.

The workflow begins with a sky position and field of view. Sphere X retrieves the corresponding SPHEREx observations and prepares them for comparison by processing the scientific image data, accounting for data-quality information, and spatially aligning observations to a common reference. Users can then move through the available epochs as a temporal sequence.

Several visualization modes make changes easier to recognize. Normal mode allows users to inspect each epoch individually; Blink rapidly alternates between two observations; Overlay combines observations using different color channels; and Difference highlights changes between compatible observations. Together, these tools make apparent motion, brightness variations, and other temporal changes easier to inspect.

Sphere X also includes an automated candidate-analysis system that can highlight sources showing possible motion or temporal variation. This system is intentionally used as an assistance tool rather than an astronomical anomaly classifier. A moving point in an image is not automatically a discovery: it may correspond to a known source, an instrumental effect, noise, or another phenomenon that requires further analysis.

To preserve human judgment, Sphere X introduces a human-in-the-loop reporting workflow. Users can select an interesting source directly in the viewer, review it across multiple epochs, classify the type of change they believe they observed, and generate a structured report containing the coordinates, observations, epochs, visualization context, and supporting notes. The goal is to turn a visual observation into reproducible evidence rather than a simple screenshot.

An AI-powered guide makes the platform accessible to people without professional astronomy experience. Because the assistant receives contextual information about the region, selected observations, visualization mode, and candidate being inspected, it can explain what the user is seeing and guide them step by step through the interface. It can teach concepts such as RA/Dec, epochs, detectors, Blink, Overlay, and Difference while the user works with real SPHEREx data.

Sphere X was developed as a web application using Svelte, TypeScript, Vite, Python, FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, and HTTPX, with scientific FITS data obtained through NASA/IPAC IRSA.

Our creative approach is to combine scientific visualization, automated assistance, AI-guided learning, and human participation in a single workflow. Rather than hiding the complexity of the data or claiming automated scientific discoveries, Sphere X helps users understand the evidence, investigate changes themselves, and participate responsibly in the exploration of the dynamic sky.
